idiom_name: typed view registry + discriminated union of view states (framework containers as the library form)
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds the one thing a JavaScript view registry lacks - a machine-checked contract between handler and views: model the open views as a discriminated union of view states, keep the registry as a Map<ViewId, ViewState> and let rendering be a switch on the discriminator, so adding a view type turns every missed case into a compile error. Framework forms of the same role are often better when the UI belongs to a framework: Angular's ViewContainerRef is literally a container of attached views (createComponent, insert, move, remove, indexOf), and React Router's Outlet renders whichever route matches, so registry and switching already exist and only the model-to-view sync - a store plus selectors - remains yours. The hand-written registry is still justified in framework-free DOM code, or when views are created dynamically outside the router's model; in both cases the union type, not the class, is what enforces the pattern.
pitfalls: Type guarantees stop at the boundary: a view type that arrives as a string from a URL or config must be validated against the union (or a schema) before the factory indexes a map with it, or the failure moves to run time.
The Map holds view state strongly, so delete() on close is the only thing that keeps the closed view's state and any DOM it references from staying reachable.
Framework containers (ViewContainerRef, Outlet) attach and detach views on their own schedule; a parallel registry creates two sources of truth about what is open and they will disagree.
Moving DOM nodes between containers loses scroll and focus state unless that state is stored outside the DOM.
